title: You Hooked A Goliath Off The Pier
body: A whole fish for bait, dropped between the pilings of a Florida fishing pier, and an Atlantic goliath grouper takes it. Goliath grouper can reach about 800 lb and over 8 ft, and adults like structure such as bridges, piers and wrecks (FWC). Hooked goliath often run for the pilings, where the jagged edges can cut the line, so pier anglers use heavy leaders and strong drag early in the fight (Waypoint TV). FWC: do not remove large goliath grouper from the water; the skeleton of a large goliath cannot support its weight out of the water, and the fish may suffer fatal injuries. Harvest was closed in Florida in 1990. Since spring 2023, Florida allows a small permit harvest in state waters: up to 200 permits a year by lottery, fish 24-36 inches only, March 1 - May 31; goliath over 36 inches stay protected (FWC, 2022 news release). Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown. Sources: myfwc.com (goliath grouper page; news release 3 Mar 2022) · waypointtv.com.

title: The Hook Before Hooks: How a Bone Gorge Locks
body: Before fishhooks had a bend, people caught fish with a gorge: a short, straight sliver of bone (or horn or hard wood), sharp at both ends, with the line tied around a groove in the middle.
How it works:
1. The gorge goes into the bait lengthwise, in line with the line, so it slides down easily.
2. A fish swallows the bait and the gorge whole.
3. A pull on the line drags the middle. The sliver swings crosswise, and both points catch in the throat.
A real bone gorge from Illinois in the Penn Museum collection is 4.78 cm long: under 2 inches.
A gorge is usually swallowed deep, so it is not catch-and-release gear. Check your local fishing rules before you try one.

Sources: Penn Museum (object 29-112-756), US National Park Service (South Florida Collections), Field & Stream, Encyclopaedia Britannica (via Wikipedia, "Fish hook"). The cutaway is a cartoon; the gorge, bait and fish are drawn larger than life, and sizes are illustrative.
Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown.

title: 7 Rookie Fishing Fails Everyone Notices
body: Seven rookie fishing fails, each one shown wrong and then right:
1. A rod loose in the truck bed bangs around, and tips can break. Strap it down or use a rack.
2. A sloppy knot slips. Learn a real hook knot: improved clinch, Palomar or uni.
3. A spinning reel hangs under the rod, with the reel stem between your fingers.
4. The clip on a spinning-reel spool only holds the line end for storage. Tie on with an arbor knot around the spool.
5. A drag cranked down tight can snap the line on a hard run. A common rule of thumb: set it to about a quarter to a third of the line's rated strength, so it slips first.
6. Braid is easy to see under water. Many anglers add a fluorocarbon leader (lower visibility, better abrasion resistance), joined with an FG, Albright or uni-to-uni knot.
7. A hook parked in a rod guide can scratch or chip the guide ring, and a damaged ring wears the line. Use the hook keeper; with no keeper, hook the guide foot, not the ring.

Sources: Salt Strong (rods in a truck bed), Field & Stream and Oregon Department of Fish and Wildlife (hook knots), Fly Fisherman (why knots slip), Minnesota DNR and Daiwa (holding a spinning rod), Field & Stream (line keeper) and Animated Knots (arbor knot), Sport Fishing (drag setting), Game & Fish, Field & Stream and Berkley (braid and fluorocarbon), FishTalk and In-Fisherman (hook keepers). Sizes are drawn larger than real so each detail reads on a phone.
Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown.

title: This Lure Has No Hook
body: Anglers catch longnose gar with a rope lure: a short piece of nylon rope, frayed into fine strands, with no hook. Missouri Department of Conservation: "A novel approach to catching gar, longnose gar in particular, is to use a rope lure." Why: "there is next to nothing in a gar's beak to set a hook into" (MDC). "When a gar grabs the lure, the nylon filaments tangle in the teeth and around the jaws of the fish." A longnose gar has needle-sharp teeth in single rows; West Virginia DNR also describes the hookless frayed rope. Caveats: a hook can hold in the corner of a gar's mouth, and many anglers use hooks and bait. Rope lures work for longnose, shortnose and spotted gar, not well for alligator gar (Mississippi Sportsman, also the source of "the more they fight, the worse they get tangled"). The duty: remove the rope before you release the fish. Illinois DNR: "If an angler just cut the line and released the gar with a tangled up snout, the fish would surely die." In-Fisherman: "Remove all the thread from the fish's mouth before releasing it." MDC: take "a small sharp knife or pair of scissors" to cut the rope away. Check the local fishing rules before you use a rope lure. The talking gar is a joke; the lure and the fibres are drawn larger than life. Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown. Sources: mdc.mo.gov (Angling for Oddball Fish; longnose gar field guide) · wvdnr.gov (longnose gar) · dnr.illinois.gov (OutdoorIllinois, June 2007) · in-fisherman.com · ms-sportsman.com · dwr.virginia.gov · floridamuseum.ufl.edu.

title: He Bit Your Arm To Guard His Eggs
body: Noodling is fishing with your bare hand: you reach into a hole and a catfish bites your arm. The fish that bites is usually a male on guard. Male flathead catfish stay with the eggs, fan them with the tail and defend the nest; a nest can hold from a few thousand up to about 100,000 eggs. In a Missouri Department of Conservation test, all the eggs in nests with no parent were dead within 12 hours, which is why hand fishing is illegal in Missouri. Cartoon; the talking catfish is fiction. Sources: Missouri Department of Conservation, Outdoor Life, Field & Stream.

title: Your Broken Line Tells You Who Did It
body: When a line breaks on a big fish, the end you reel back in is a clue. These are anglers' rules of thumb, not lab tests. 1) A tight curl or "pigtail" on the end: the knot slipped and pulled loose. The Fishing Manual: "If it comes back with a tight little curl at the end, a pigtail, your knot slipped." Pittsburgh Post-Gazette (John Hayes, 2017): the hookup was solid and the line was strong, "leaving nothing but the weak knot's curly remains." Fix: wet the knot, cinch it fully, leave a short tag. 2) A rough or frayed end: the line wore through. The Fishing Manual: "If your line breaks somewhere out in the middle, that is abrasion or a nick" - line "dragged over rock, rubbed against a dock post, or chewed by a fish." Braid frays; mono and fluorocarbon show nicks and rough spots. Run the last few feet of line through your fingers and cut back past any roughness. 3) A clean cut with the lure gone, while fishing for pike: a bite-off. Iowa DNR: "Pike have rows of sharp teeth that can easily cut through most fishing line." In-Fisherman (Matt Straw): "I've witnessed clean bite-offs with fluorocarbon." Caveat: a clean, straight end right at the knot can also mean the knot itself broke (The Fishing Manual). The fix for pike: Iowa DNR: "Leaders made from wire, steel or titanium can protect your line from being bitten off." Minnesota DNR: "Don't forget a steel leader for larger pikes." Many pike anglers also use heavy fluorocarbon leaders, but pike can bite through those too. Line ends, lure and line are drawn larger than life; the line is shown in hi-vis yellow. Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown. Sources: thefishingmanual.com (Why Fishing Knots Fail) · Pittsburgh Post-Gazette via vnews.com (Tie it right and tight, 2017) · iowadnr.gov (northern pike) · dnr.state.mn.us (northern pike profile) · in-fisherman.com (Fishing Leader Options; Fluorocarbon Secrets for Pike) · sportfishingmag.com (abrasion).

title: Never Throw This Fish Back
body: What to do when you catch a northern snakehead in the eastern United States. It is native to East Asia; the first breeding US population was found in 2002 in a pond in Crofton, Maryland, from released live food-market fish (Maryland DNR, USGS). It breathes air and "can also survive out of the water for several days if their skin remains moist" (Maryland DNR; USFWS: up to four days). It does not walk. Maryland DNR: females average about 40,000 eggs, and both parents guard the young. The rules are not the same in every state. USFWS: "Anglers are asked to NOT RELEASE Northern Snakehead alive." New York: a snakehead "cannot be released back into the water. They must be immediately killed and reported to DEC." Maryland and Virginia do not require you to kill one that you release at once in the same water, but both ask you to kill it, and it is illegal to keep or move a live one (also in Pennsylvania and Delaware; the federal Lacey Act prohibits import and interstate transport of live snakeheads). Virginia asks you to report a kept fish. In 2024 Maryland made "Chesapeake Channa" the state name of the fish to help sell it as food. Do not confuse it with the native bowfin: a snakehead has a long anal fin and no tail spot. Check the current rule of your state before you fish. Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown. Sources: fws.gov (northern snakehead) · dnr.maryland.gov (snakehead) · dwr.virginia.gov/fishing/snakehead · dec.ny.gov · pa.gov (Fish and Boat Commission) · dnrec.delaware.gov.

title: This Decoy Tells You How Big The Pike Is
body: Dark house spearing in Minnesota: a dark house has no windows (or covered ones), so the fish and the lake bottom show up in the viewing hole and the fish cannot see you (Minnesota DNR). On Lake of the Woods and the Rainy River, all northern pike from 30 through 40 inches must be released immediately, and one pike longer than 40 inches may be kept (Minnesota DNR, Information for Pike Spearers; Lake of the Woods page). The DNR tip: use a large decoy of known length as a ruler; with a 15-inch decoy, a pike is legal to spear there if it is less than twice the decoy's length. Another DNR guide: if the snout-to-gill distance is 6.2 inches, you can be about 98% sure the pike is under 30 inches. And: if you are in doubt about the size, you do not have to spear it. Size rules differ by water and zone in Minnesota; check the current regulations for your lake. No fish is speared or harmed in this video. Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown. Sources: dnr.state.mn.us (Information for Pike Spearers, Baudette area office; Ice fishing: northern pike spearing; Lake of the Woods).

title: Ranking 5 Fish By How Hard They Hit Your Bait
body: Five fish, ranked by how they hit a bait, from the softest take to the most violent. #5 Catfish: channel catfish have taste buds over their whole body, most around the whiskers (USFWS, North Dakota Game and Fish); a cat often grabs the bait and swims off while the rod loads up slowly (In-Fisherman). #4 Walleye: often just a light tap, or a slight weight on the line (In-Fisherman). #3 Largemouth bass: it expands its mouth to draw prey in, in less than 30 milliseconds (DeVries & Wainwright 2006, UC Davis). #2 Northern pike: a lie-in-wait predator that ambushes from weedbeds, clutches prey sideways and turns it head-first before swallowing (Minnesota DNR); prey-capture fast-starts last about 0.08 s (Harper & Blake 1991). #1 Yellowfin tuna: when a big yellowfin hits a live bait, line screams off the reel (Game & Fish); tunas have been seen swimming at about 28 mph over long distances (LSU / Louisiana Sea Grant; that figure is for tunas in general). The order is our own ranking of typical takes; every bite varies. Sizes and scenes are illustrative. Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown.

title: Never Pull A Big Halibut Into Your Boat
body: Why anglers subdue a big Pacific halibut before it comes into the boat. Alaska Department of Fish and Game: the maximum reported size is over 8 feet and over 500 pounds; some anglers dispatch a large halibut with a handgun before boating it, others use a gaff, shark hook or harpoon attached to a strong rope and float. Alaska sport regulations permit a firearm on a vessel in salt water to dispatch a fish caught with legal gear. The International Pacific Halibut Commission wrote that halibut are powerful and have been known to smash objects with their tails, and reprinted an Alaska Empire report (Juneau, August 1973, headline "Fisherman Killed By Halibut") about a 150-pound halibut. Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown or named. Sources: adfg.alaska.gov, IPHC Technical Report 16 (1978).

title: A Giant Pike Grabbed My Hooked Pike
body: Pike eat pike. Larger northern pike also eat smaller northern pike (Wisconsin DNR; Minnesota DNR: "Large pike sometimes eat smaller pike"). Minnesota DNR calls the pike a lie-in-wait predator that takes any living thing up to about a third of its body length that will go down its throat, with hundreds of backward-slanting teeth to grip. Wisconsin DNR: it lurks alone amid weed beds, then lunges out and snatches prey. The Game & Wildlife Conservation Trust: pike catch prey sideways in the mouth, hold it with their teeth, then turn it head first to swallow. Lab work (Nilsson & Brönmark 1999, Behavioral Ecology 10:557-566) found that pike that strike and swallow prey head first handle it faster. Caveat: this is an illustrated example of a behaviour anglers report, not one recorded event; the big pike is not hooked, and big pike that grab a hooked fish often let go near the boat, but not always. Sizes are illustrative. Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown. Sources: dnr.state.mn.us (Species Profile: Northern Pike) · dnr.wisconsin.gov (Northern pike) · gwct.org.uk (Pike, species of the month) · Behavioral Ecology (1999).

title: He Found A Finger Inside His Trout
body: A true story from Priest Lake, Idaho. On 11 September 2012 an angler caught a lake trout, and when he cleaned it he found a human finger inside. He put it on ice and the Bonner County Sheriff's Office took a fingerprint from it; the Idaho State Police lab confirmed the match. The finger belonged to a wakeboarder who lost four fingers of his left hand on 21 June 2012, when his hand caught in the tow rope, about eight miles from the place where the fish was caught. The sheriff's office offered to return it; he told reporters his answer was "uhhh, I'm good". The detective said: "There's still three more, too." Nobody is named in the video. The characters are generic cartoon figures, not likenesses of the real people; the phone words in the yellow bubble follow the wakeboarder's own account ("he had a strange story to tell me"). Nothing graphic is shown. Sources: The Spokesman-Review, 26 Sep 2012 ("Lake trout yields boarder's lost finger") · AP via CBS News, 25 Sep 2012.

title: They Took The Bait Off The Hook
body: Carp don't bite like a pike: a carp sucks food in, sorts it in its mouth and spits out what it doesn't want (Callan & Sanderson 2003, Journal of Experimental Biology, on grit and food particles). A bait with the hook buried inside it can be felt and blown back out before the angler can strike. The fix: the hair rig, credited to Len Middleton and Kevin Maddocks in England in the late 1970s (American Carp Society; Carpology dates the original hair before 1980; Wikipedia says it became popular in the 1980s). The bait sits on a fine 'hair' next to a bare hook. The carp sucks in bait and hook together; when it tries to blow the bait out, the hook drops and usually catches in the bottom lip. With a heavy semi-fixed lead (a bolt rig) the fish feels the weight, 'the lead drives the hook home and makes it bolt' (Korda), and the bite alarm sounds: no strike needed (Wikipedia: 'a very effective self-hooking rig'). The first hairs were real human hair (Wikipedia). Caveats: dates differ by source; bottom-lip hook holds are typical, not certain; use a lead safety clip so the lead can drop free if the line breaks. The rig is drawn about 3.6 times real size under water. Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown. Sources: americancarpsociety.com (rig design) · en.wikipedia.org (Hair rig; Bite indicator) · carpology.net · kordatackle.com · anglingtimes.co.uk · fishingagain.com · Callan & Sanderson 2003 (J Exp Biol).

title: The Biggest Fish Ever Caught On A Rod
body: Seven all-tackle world-record fish next to the same angler, from the smallest to the biggest. Bluegill 4 lb 12 oz (T.S. Hudson, Ketona Lake, Alabama, 1950). Largemouth bass 22 lb 4 oz (George Perry, Georgia, 1932; tied in Japan in 2009). Muskellunge 67 lb 8 oz (Cal Johnson, Wisconsin, 1949; this record is disputed, but IGFA keeps it). Flathead catfish 123 lb (Ken Paulie, Elk City Reservoir, Kansas, 1998). Tarpon 286 lb 9 oz (Max Domecq, Guinea-Bissau, 2003). Atlantic bluefin tuna 1,496 lb (Ken Fraser, Nova Scotia, 1979; Marlin Magazine gives the fight as 45 minutes, IGFA as just under an hour). White shark 2,664 lb (Alfred Dean, off Ceduna, South Australia, April 1959, on 130-pound line): the heaviest fish that IGFA has certified on rod and reel. A ton here is the US ton (2,000 lb). The fish lengths in the drawing are approximate. Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown. Sources: igfa.org (20 Enduring IGFA World Records) · myfwc.com (tarpon records) · gameandfishmag.com · outdoorlife.com (the biggest fish caught) · saltwatersportsman.com · marlinmag.com.

title: Throw A Huge Bait, Get A Huge Catfish
body: A fish chunk the size of a sandwich, on a big circle hook, on the bottom of a river. Small fish peck at it but cannot swallow it; a big blue catfish can. Big baits usually get fewer bites, but the fish that does bite is more often a big one (In-Fisherman, "Livebait Tactics for Blue Catfish": "Big livebaits usually don't account for a lot of action, but when a fish bites it's probably a good one"; Missouri Conservationist, "Catching Big River Blues": a big blue "might swim right by that penny, but it rarely ignores a quarter"). Circle hooks are designed to hook fish in the corner of the mouth (Missouri Dept. of Conservation; Maryland DNR). Blue catfish commonly reach 20 to 40 pounds and can top 100 pounds (Texas Parks & Wildlife). Virginia's state record blue catfish weighed 143 lb (Buggs Island Lake, 2011; Virginia DWR). Caveats: big baits also catch small catfish, and small baits also catch big ones; the 46-inch length on the tape is our illustration, not a measured fish. Where blue catfish are invasive (for example Maryland), local rules ask anglers to keep them; check your local regulations. Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown.

title: This Fish Bites Right At Your Feet
body: A muskie explains the figure-eight. Wisconsin DNR: muskies often show themselves by following a lure back to the boat without striking, so experienced anglers use a figure-8 with the lure at boat-side to provoke a strike. Missouri MDC: do not lift the lure out; put the rod tip in the water and move it in a large, wide figure-eight. Outdoor News: keep the turns wide, because muskies don't corner well. The muskie is called the fish of 10,000 casts (MDC, US Fish & Wildlife Service) and is an ambush predator with burst speeds of 30 miles per hour (USFWS). The talking fish is fiction; the behaviour is sourced. Sources: dnr.wisconsin.gov, mdc.mo.gov, fws.gov, outdoornews.com.

title: You Just Stepped On A Sleeping Stingray
body: Round stingrays rest on the bottom and blend in with the sand in the shallow surf of Southern California (ABC7, 29 Jun 2023). They only sting in self-defense (NPR via WUSF, 2014). A CSULB biology professor told ABC7 that a ray pinned down in the centre will most likely strike about 85% of the time. The fix is the stingray shuffle: slide your feet along the sand so you nudge a ray and it swims off, instead of stepping on it. Stings are treated by soaking in hot water, as hot as the person can safely tolerate; the heat breaks down the toxin (ABC7; KTLA). At Seal Beach, California, Marine Safety Chief Joe Bailey said there are more than 30,000 rays in the area by the San Gabriel River (ABC7, 2023). In July 2025 he told KTLA that lifeguards typically treat about one sting a day, but the number had climbed to around a dozen a day (KTLA, 31 Jul 2025). Sting counts vary by year: ABC7 reported more than 500 a year in 2023, NPR about 400 a year in 2014. Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown. The talking stingray is fiction. Sources: abc7.com (29 Jun 2023), KTLA via yahoo.com (31 Jul 2025), wusf.org / NPR (21 Jan 2014).

title: The Bass Got Off. The Hook Didn't
body: A largemouth bass shook free, and the other treble of the crankbait ended up in your thumb. The bass tells you what happens next. Why you should not just pull it straight back: behind the point sits the barb, and doctors are told to stop if the barb catches during a backward pull (American Family Physician). For a hook that is NOT deep, doctors use the string-yank method: a loop of fishing line around the middle of the bend, the shank pressed down against the skin, then one firm, quick jerk along the shank (American Family Physician; MedlinePlus). The hook can come out fast: keep everyone's face out of its line of flight. Do NOT try it if the hook is deep, in a joint or tendon, or in or near an eye, eyelid or artery: get medical help (MedlinePlus). A hook in the eye is an emergency. If your tetanus shot is not up to date, call your doctor. This is not medical advice and it does not always work. Pliers can crimp a barb flat, and a barbless hook comes out of a fish more easily (South Carolina DNR). Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown. Sources: Gammons & Jackson, Am Fam Physician 2001 'Fishhook Removal' · MedlinePlus 'Removing a fish hook' · SC DNR 'Using Barbless Hooks'.

title: One Bite Cost This Crew $3.5 Million
body: The true story of the 2023 Big Rock Blue Marlin Tournament (Morehead City, North Carolina; 271 boats; purse $5,835,075). In the final hour of the final day a crew hooked a blue marlin and fought it for more than six hours. At the scales it weighed 619.4 lb, 134.9 lb more than any other fish that week and the only marlin above 500 lb. It would have won about $3.5 million ($2.77 million first place plus the $739,500 prize for the first marlin above 500 lb). The next morning the tournament said the fish "is disqualified due to mutilation caused by a shark or other marine animal" before it was landed (tournament rule 23, taken from IGFA rules). A 484.5 lb marlin won $2,769,437.50. The crew protested, then withdrew the protest on 11 July 2023 and said the tournament "made the correct decision". Cartoon illustration: no real person is shown, the boats and figures are generic, and the position and shape of the bite mark are an illustration (reports do not agree on where it was). Sources: thebigrock.com (65th annual tournament results) · Washington Post / boston.com, 19 June 2023 · cbsnews.com · islandfreepress.org · witn.com, 11 July 2023.

title: A Grouper Swallowed His Shark Whole
body: In August 2014 anglers off Bonita Springs, Florida, had a blacktip shark of about 4 feet at the boat when a goliath grouper came up and swallowed it in one gulp. Goliath grouper can grow past 8 feet and 800 pounds (Florida Museum). They do not cut prey: they open the mouth so fast that water rushes in and the prey is pulled in and swallowed whole (US Fish & Wildlife Service). Florida wildlife officers say goliath grouper feed on fish that struggle on a fishing line. Cartoon reconstruction; no real person is shown. Sources: KSL / Good Morning America (Aug 2014), Florida Museum, USFWS, Florida FWC.

title: Some Bass Are Born Hard To Catch
body: Why some bass never bite. At Ridge Lake, Illinois, University of Illinois / Illinois Natural History Survey scientists ran four seasons of fully controlled catch-and-release fishing in the late 1970s: every bass caught was measured, tagged and released. Then the lake was drained. More than 1,700 bass were collected, and about 200 of them had never been caught in four years. One bass was caught 16 times in a single year. The scientists then bred never-caught bass and often-caught bass (caught 4 or more times) apart for three generations over about 20 years. The offspring of often-caught parents were caught more, and the offspring of never-caught parents were harder to catch: "vulnerability was a heritable trait" (Philipp, Cooke, Claussen, Koppelman, Suski & Burkett 2009, Transactions of the American Fisheries Society 138:189-199). Catchability is only partly inherited (realized heritability about 0.15); learning and conditions also matter. The last line is the authors' own point: when anglers keep the easy-to-catch bass, the hard-to-catch ones are left to breed. Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown. Sources: eurekalert.org (University of Illinois release, 2009) · sciencedaily.com (2009-04-14) · Transactions of the American Fisheries Society 138:189-199.

title: Bass Usually Turn A Bluegill Around First
body: Why a largemouth bass turns a bluegill before it swallows it. A bass can grab a fish crosswise, then turn it and swallow it head first. In a gastroscope study of 810 Oklahoma largemouth bass (Zweiacker & Summerfelt, Proc. Southeastern Assoc. Game & Fish Commissioners), 66.4% of fresh gizzard shad in 137 stomachs had gone down head first, which the authors explain by the bass turning its prey before swallowing (Lawrence 1958). Their reason: head first, the median fins fold flat; spiny fins the other way would probably injure the predator. The same study: crayfish went down tail first in 96.8% of 93 stomachs, so the claws fold. Maryland DNR: the front of the bluegill dorsal fin has 9 to 12 sharp spines that make it hard for predators to swallow (Texas Parks & Wildlife: usually 10). Caveats: usually, not always; small prey can go down either way; the study prey was shad, not bluegill. The swimbait tip is an angler inference, not a study result. Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown. Sources: seafwa.org (Zweiacker & Summerfelt) · dnr.maryland.gov (Biology of Bluegill) · tpwd.texas.gov (Bluegill).

title: I Took Your Fish And Dragged You 20 Feet
body: On a June dive at a shipwreck off Apalachicola, Florida, spearfisher Grayson Shepard was spearing snapper when goliath groupers tried to take his catch. One grabbed his speared fish; he held on, and he said: "I weigh 220 pounds, and it dragged me easily 20 feet or so before letting go." A grouper also bent his spear "so badly it will no longer load into my speargun" (National Geographic, 5 Nov 2015; UPI, 6 Nov 2015). The reports do not say he was hurt. Goliath grouper grow up to about 8 feet and 800 pounds, the largest grouper in western Atlantic waters; they catch prey by a rapid opening of the mouth that sucks it in to be swallowed whole (Florida FWC). They make a rumbling sound with the swim bladder and show intruders an open mouth and a quivering body; very large goliaths have been seen to stalk divers (Florida Museum of Natural History). Protected from harvest in US waters since 1990; Florida now allows a small, permit-only harvest (FWC). The 20-foot distance is the diver's own estimate. Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown. The talking grouper is fiction.

title: You Were Standing In Our Lunch
body: Bluefish feed in big schools that drive bait fish to the surface and churn the water; NOAA Fisheries calls it a bluefish blitz. Maryland DNR says bluefish have razor sharp triangular teeth, are known as the "marine piranha" and have occasionally bitten swimmers who met a feeding school. Marine biologists quoted by the AP say bluefish are not man-eaters but sometimes bite people by mistake while they chase bait fish near the shore. July 2009, Sagaponack, New York: at least two surfers were taken to Southampton Hospital with bites to their feet, and several other people had less serious bites to their feet and hands, from bluefish feeding on bait pushed toward shore by storms (East Hampton Press, 29 Jul 2009). July 2010, Hither Hills State Park, Montauk: a school of bluefish bit two swimmers, one on the foot and one on the hand, and lifeguards cleared the water (AP via NBC New York, 10 Jul 2010). Maryland DNR describes such bites as occasional. Cartoon illustration; no real person is shown. The talking bluefish is fiction. Sources: fisheries.noaa.gov, dnr.maryland.gov, deq.nc.gov, 27east.com, nbcnewyork.com.
